skill.name: code-craft
skill.description: Guides code writing, review, refactoring, and project setup with durable engineering principles for Rust, TypeScript, Go, and Python.
skill.summary: Apply practical type, error, testing, architecture, and simplicity principles across four programming languages.
skill.author: jssblck

security_audit.summary: Most static detections are false positives caused by Markdown links, inline code formatting, or explanatory engineering prose. Two installer examples genuinely recommend immediate execution of remote scripts through Bash or PowerShell.

remediation.issue: Remote install commands execute downloaded scripts immediately through Bash or PowerShell.
remediation.suggestion: Show separate download, signature or checksum verification, inspection, and execution steps for both installer scripts.

content.user_title: Build Reliable Code with Durable Principles
content.value_statement: Inconsistent engineering choices make code harder to review and maintain. This skill applies clear design, testing, error, and tooling defaults across common languages.
actual_capabilities: Applies language-independent principles for types, parsing, errors, testing, architecture, and simplicity.
Maps those principles to Rust, TypeScript, Go, and Python idioms.
Reviews code for weak invariants, stringly typed data, hidden failures, and premature abstractions.
Guides behavior-focused tests using real boundaries, temporary resources, and property-based testing.
Recommends formatter, linter, type-checking, CI, and pre-commit defaults for new projects.
Routes deeper questions to focused principle and language guidance.
limitations: It provides guidance rather than a compiler, linter, or test runner.
It supports four languages directly; other languages receive only the universal principles.
Its opinionated defaults may conflict with established repository conventions.
Project-specific security, performance, and compliance requirements still require expert review.

use_cases.title: Review a Pull Request
use_cases.description: Identify design, error-handling, testing, and maintainability issues with language-specific recommendations.

use_cases.title: Refactor a Legacy Module
use_cases.description: Replace weak boundaries and primitive values with parsed, explicit domain types.

use_cases.title: Bootstrap Project Standards
use_cases.description: Select consistent formatting, linting, testing, CI, and governance defaults for a new repository.

prompt_templates.title: Check a Function
prompt_templates.prompt: Review this [language] function for clear errors, strong types, and simple control flow. Explain the most important changes.
prompt_templates.scenario: A beginner wants focused feedback on a small function.

prompt_templates.title: Improve Test Design
prompt_templates.prompt: Review these [language] tests. Focus on observable behavior, realistic boundaries, deterministic execution, and unnecessary mocking. Propose specific improvements.
prompt_templates.scenario: A developer wants more durable tests.

prompt_templates.title: Refactor a Module
prompt_templates.prompt: Refactor this [language] module using parsed boundaries, explicit domain types, and errors as values. Preserve behavior and follow existing repository conventions.
prompt_templates.scenario: A maintainer is improving an existing module.

prompt_templates.title: Design a Project Baseline
prompt_templates.prompt: Design standards for a new [language] project. Include formatting, linting, type checks, tests, CI, pre-commit checks, architecture notes, and release safeguards.
prompt_templates.scenario: A technical lead needs a complete engineering baseline.

output_examples.input: Review a TypeScript checkout function that accepts untyped request data and throws generic errors.
output: Parse request data once at the boundary into explicit checkout types.
Represent expected failures with a typed result instead of generic exceptions.
Add behavior tests for invalid items, missing payment data, and declined payments.

output_examples.input: Recommend a Python project quality baseline for a small command-line application.
output: Use Ruff for formatting and linting, plus strict static type checking.
Run formatting, linting, typing, and tests through one shared command.
Call the same command from local pre-commit checks and continuous integration.

best_practices: Provide the target language, repository conventions, and relevant code or diff.
Ask for behavior preservation and require formatter, type-checker, linter, and test verification.
Apply recommendations selectively when established project rules require a different approach.
anti_patterns: Do not request broad rewrites without defining behavior and scope.
Do not apply new abstractions before identifying real callers and duplicated needs.
Do not treat generated advice as proof that tests, security, or performance are correct.

faq.question: Which languages receive detailed guidance?
faq.answer: Rust, TypeScript, Go, and Python receive dedicated idioms, tooling, testing, and project-layout guidance.

faq.question: Can it review existing code?
faq.answer: Yes. It can assess code or diffs against its design, error, testing, and simplicity principles.

faq.question: Can it scaffold a new project?
faq.answer: It can recommend project defaults and structure, but the coding agent performs the actual file changes.

faq.question: Does it replace project instructions?
faq.answer: No. Repository instructions and established conventions take precedence over this skill.

faq.question: Does it run tests and linters?
faq.answer: No. It instructs the coding agent to run the repository tools and report verification results.

faq.question: Does it guarantee secure code?
faq.answer: No. Its principles can improve boundaries and failure handling, but dedicated security review remains necessary.
